definition: Heterogeneity means the state of being made up of parts that differ in kind — variety running all the way through one group or mixture.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word heterogeneity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know heterogeneity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Geologists prize the cliff face for its heterogeneity: sandstone, shale, and volcanic ash stacked in bands, each laid down by a different age.

Variety is milder than heterogeneity: variety promises a pleasing surface assortment — several flavors, a few styles — while heterogeneity says the parts of the group differ more deeply, down to their very kinds.

Incongruity goes further than heterogeneity: a group can show heterogeneity and still work as one whole, but incongruity means the differences have sharpened into a clash, and the pieces no longer seem to belong together.

Diversity is variety among the people or things in a group, and usually a word of welcome — a diverse newsroom, a diverse diet. Heterogeneity measures the same mixedness coolly, without applause, and insists the differences reach down to kind.

Variability is how much something changes across measurements or over time - one river's depth through the seasons. Heterogeneity is difference across the parts of one group at one time: not a value moving, but a mixture of unlike members.
Dissimilarity is the plain fact that two things are unlike each other. Heterogeneity scales that unlikeness up to a whole collection: one group whose many parts differ among themselves.

The anthology's pieces do not simply vary in topic — they belong to different species of writing altogether — and the word reports that all-the-way-down difference precisely, without praising or blaming it.
Heterogeneity belongs to lab reports, census tables, and policy reviews: samples, populations, and portfolios have heterogeneity.
Everyday speech reaches for variety or diversity instead.
Choose it when you are measuring a mixture rather than celebrating one - and keep its mirror straight: its clean opposite, "uniformity," is taught in this same unit.

The sorting machines at the county recycling plant were designed for a tidy stream: bottles, cans, paper.
What arrives instead is a torrent of unlike things - laptop chargers, garden hoses, ceramic mugs, bowling balls.
Engineers call the problem the heterogeneity of the waste stream, and it defeats automation more reliably than volume ever has.
A ballistic separator can shake paper from plastic, but no machine yet built expects a bowling ball; the parts of the stream differ not in amount but in kind.
The plant's fix is human: forty sorters who can recognize anything.
Machines handle sameness, the manager says.
